is an effective strategy to enhance CO2ER performance, as it can tune the binding energy between intermediates and catalysts, leading to the enhanced reaction kinetics of CO2ER.[3] For example, Yin et al. investigated palladium–copper (Pd–Cu) alloy catalysts on CO2ER and found that Pd85Cu15/C showed the highest CO faradaic efficiency (FE) of 86% at −0.89 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE).[4] Besides, the introduction of high-indexed facets has also been reported to be an alternative way to facilitate CO2ER performance.[5] Au nanowires[6] and Ag nanoplates[7] with more edge sites exhibited preference on CO; tiny-sized Pd nanoparticles (NPs)[8] with more edge and terrace sites also showed enhanced CO FE.
Therefore, combining alloying with exposing low-coordinated sites should be a promising way to further enhance CO2ER performance. Recently, AgPd nanoden-
drite-modified Au prisms showed high electrocatalytic performance toward CO2ER and achieved tunable product distribution from formate to CO as the Pd content varies.[9] However, the reaction mechanism of CO2ER performance on AgPd–Au still needs to be further investigated by experiments or corresponding theories. Up till now, it is still a great challenge to precisely control the specific morphology of alloy catalysts and to elucidate their complex reaction mechanism.[10]
This paper describes a facile way to synthesize a series of shape-controlled Pd–Cu nanocatalysts. Among them, remarkable CH4 current density and CO current density are achieved by concave rhombic dodecahedral Cu3Pd (CRD-Cu3Pd) and flower-like Pd3Cu (FL-Pd3Cu) catalysts, respectively. In addition to the achievement of excellent catalytic performance and tunable product distribution, we further explore the reaction pathway systematically via the combination of experiments and density functional theory (DFT) calculations.
The Pd–Cu bimetallic nanocrystals (NCs) were obtained by a modified wet-chemical reduction method previously reported by Zeng and co-workers.[11] One-pot synthesis of catalysts was achieved by using Na2PdCl4 and CuCl2·2H2O as metal sources and glucose as the reductant with the presence of hexadecylamine (HDA). By simply varying the Cu and Pd precursor ratio, six types of Pd–Cu NCs with different morphologies were
Electrochemical conversion of carbon dioxide (electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide) to value-added products is a promising way to solve CO2 emission problems. This paper describes a facile one-pot approach to synthesize palladium–copper (Pd–Cu) bimetallic catalysts with different structures. Highly efficient performance and tunable product distributions are achieved due to a coordinative function of both enriched low-coordinated sites and composition effects. The concave rhombic dodecahedral Cu3Pd (CRD-Cu3Pd) decreases the onset potential for methane (CH4) by 200 mV and shows a sevenfold CH4 current density at −1.2 V (vs reversible hydrogen electrode) compared to Cu foil. The flower-like Pd3Cu (FL-Pd3Cu) exhibits high faradaic efficiency toward CO in a wide potential range from −0.7 to −1.3 V, and reaches a fourfold CO current density at −1.3 V compared to commercial Pd black. Tafel plots and density functional theory calculations suggest that both the introduction of high-index facets and alloying contribute to the enhanced CH4 current of CRD-Cu3Pd, while the alloy effect is responsible for high CO selectivity of FL-Pd3Cu.

sections.heading: CO2 Electroreduction
sections.text:
The electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2ER) is an emerging route for curbing the exceeding CO2 emissions and producing added-valued chemicals. Numerous metallic electrocatalysts have been investigated for CO2ER because their vacant orbits and active d electrons are considered to be able to effectively promote the CO2 adduct bonding with metal as well as the desorption of products.[1] However, the wide application of the catalysts is still significantly hindered by high overpotential and side reactions with the represent of the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER).[2] Several routes have been developed to improve the performance of catalysts. Among them, alloying

Scheme 1 shows the morphological evolution of NCs obtained under the Cu/Pd ratio from 0 to 3:1. It can be clearly observed that with the increase of Pd/Cu ratio, the Pd–Cu NCs evolved from uniform concave rhombic dodecahedra to irregular structures, and finally to Pd flowers with curl dendrites (Figure 1). The as-prepared CRDCu3Pd (Figure 1a) and FL-Pd3Cu (Figure 1e) NCs are uniform in both size and morphology. According to previous works, the as-prepared concave rhombic dodecahedral NCs expose high-index facets.[12] The dendritic Pd structures are consisted with {111} and part of high-index steps.[13] By performing selected area fast Fourier transform on one concave rhombic dodecahedral NC in the high-resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) image (Figure 1g), the periodic fringe spaces are confirmed to be 0.220 and 0.135 nm (Figure 1h), corresponding to the d values for the (111) and (2014) planes of Cu3Pd fcc NCs. As displayed in Figure 1j,k, the Pd3Cu alloy structure was observed with a d-spacing of 0.217 nm, which is between the (111) lattice spacing of pure Pd (0.223 nm) and Cu (0.208 nm), indicating the successful incorporation of Cu atoms into Pd lattice. The energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy mapping profiles shown in Figure 1i,l clearly reveal the homogeneous distribution of Pd and Cu elements on the concave rhombic dodecahedra and nanoflower structures. The inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES) also shows that Pd/Cu values of as-prepared catalysts are close to the ideal ratios (Table S2, Supporting Information).
We then determined the crystalline structure of Cu3Pd and Pd3Cu NCs by X-ray powder diffraction pattern (Figure S1, Supporting Information). The diffraction peaks of the two NCs appear between the peaks of pure fcc Pd and fcc Cu, indicating the formation of Pd–Cu alloy structure. In addition, the diffraction peaks obviously shifted to high angle positions with the evolution of Pd3Cu to Cu3Pd NCs, indicating more Cu content were doped in the concave rhombic dodecahedral structure. Their surface chemical composition was also characterized by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS; Figure S2, Supporting Information). Both Cu3Pd NCs and Pd3Cu NCs show peaks at Pd 3d3/2 (340.5 eV) and 3d5/2 (335.0 eV). The peaks in Cu 2p XPS spectrum at around 932.6 and 952.1 eV can be assigned to Cu(I)/ Cu(0) species; and the peaks at 943.8 eV can be assigned to Cu(II), indicating partial Cu oxidation on surface. The oxidized Cu might be reduced during the CO2ER process. Hence, the initial amount of Cu oxides on the surface has little effect on the production distribution in CO2ER.[14] The slight shifts in the binding energies of PdCu alloy compared to pure Pd and pure Cu indicates a strong electronic interaction between Pd and Cu, further confirming the formation of Pd–Cu alloy.
The morphological evolution of Pd–Cu NCs was derived from a kinetically controlled nucleation and growth process. The higher reduction potential of PdCl42− (PdCl42−/Pd: +0.591 V vs
RHE) leads to a faster reduction rate, and thus the isotropic growth, leading to the formation of flower-like structure. Conversely, higher copper content tends to manifest anisotropic growth because of the much lower reduction potential (Cu2+/ Cu:+0.34 V vs RHE). As a result, with the introduction of more Cu content, the products exhibited regular morphology. It should be pointed out that, when only Cu content was used in the growth solution, no products were obtained due to its lower reduction potential. To further elucidate the reaction kinetics influence on final morphology, the controlled experiment containing much more glucose was conducted. Figure S3 (Supporting Information) shows a near-spherical morphology of Cu3Pd NPs when the glucose amount increased from 15 to 50 mg, further proving that the higher reduction rate causes isotropic growth. In addition, the formation of specific facets could also be attributed to the thermodynamic stabilization of these facets via capping agent absorption.[15] We consider that, as an important surfactant, HDA can absorb on the (110) facets of Cu3Pd NCs and thus lead to the concave rhombic dodecahedral morphology. To confirm our assumption, we decreased HDA amount to 150 and 90 mg, respectively (Figure S4, Supporting Information).With the HDA amount decreasing, hollow structures of NPs appeared. When the capping ability from HDA became weakened, the facets of initially formed NPs become more easier to be etched. When the HDA amount was decreased to 70 mg, the solution changed to milk white, indicating that no Cu NCs or Pd NCs were formed. This phenomenon indicated that HDA not only played an important role in shaping rhombic dodecahedral morphology but also functioned as a kind of weak reducing agent.
The CO2ER electrocatalytic activity was evaluated by controlled potential electrolysis in CO2-saturated 0.1 m KHCO3 solution at 18 °C. The main products of the electrolysis were CH4, CO, and H2. A remarkably enhanced catalytic activity toward CO2 reduction to CH4 was observed on CRD-Cu3Pd NCs. The onset potential for CO2 to CH4 at CRD-Cu3Pd appears at −1.0 V, which is 200 mV more positive than that at copper foil. The maximum FE for CH4 of 40.6% was achieved at −1.2 V for CRD-Cu3Pd NCs, which is two times than that of Cu foil

(Figure 2a). Moreover, the undesirable side reaction, HER, is suppressed on CRD-Cu3Pd NCs, which exhibits a minimum FE of 25.2% at −1.2 V. For copper foil, however, H2 evolution was not well suppressed by CH4 formation. The minimum H2 FE appears at −1.2 V, not corresponding to the maximum CH4 FE. Consequently, partial current densities for CH4 on CRD-Cu3Pd NCs are about sevenfold of Cu foil at −1.2 V (Figure 2b). For the FL-Pd3Cu NCs, CO and H2 are the two gaseous products. Although the FL-Pd3Cu catalysts exhibit lower total current density than commercial Pd/C catalysts (C-Pd) at lower potential (Figure S5, Supporting Information), the current densities for FL-Pd3Cu increase rapidly at potential more negative than −0.9 V. Besides, the CO FE reaches 82.1% over FL-Pd3Cu at −0.9 V, which is significantly higher than that of 48.8% over C-Pd (Figure 2c). It is worth mentioning that FL-Pd3Cu NCs exhibit a high selectivity toward CO in a wide range from −0.7 to −1.3 V. Although the CO partial current density for FL-Pd3Cu NCs (1.2 mA cm−2) is a little lower than 1.5 mA cm−2 of C-Pd at −0.7 V, its current density exceeds C-Pd sharply at more negative potential, and finally reach 16.7 mA cm−2 at −1.3 V, which is fourfold than that of C-Pd (Figure 2d). As comparison, the pure Pd nanoflowers show almost no selectivity toward CO (Figure S6, Supporting Information). These results indicated that asprepared Cu-Pd alloy catalysts exhibited adjustable product

selectivity for CO2ER. As shown in Table S3 (Supporting Information), the CH4 and CO FE achieved on Cu3Pd and Pd3Cu catalyst are also comparable to the reported CuPd bimetallic catalysts.
To investigate the morphology stability of the catalysts, the catalysts after reaction were investigated by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). As shown in Figure S7 (Supporting Information), the Pd3Cu and Cu3Pd catalysts maintained their flower-like and rhombic dodecahedral morphologies, respectively. XPS spectral analysis of the Pd3Cu and Cu3Pd after CO2ER tests was also carried out (Figure S8, Supporting Information). The Cu3Pd NCs and Pd3Cu NCs show peaks at Pd 3d3/2 (341.0 eV) and 3d5/2 (335.7 eV). The peaks in Cu 2p XPS spectrum are at around 944.3, 933.2, and 953.2 eV. These peak locations still show minor shifts compared to pure Cu and Pd, indicating the maintained alloy structure. In addition, the peaks move to higher angles compared to that of Pd–Cu NCs before reaction, which may results from the slight segregation of Cu from core to surface.
To elucidate the enhanced CO2ER performance of nanostructured bimetallic Pd–Cu catalysts, we measured the partial current density for Tafel plots of various catalysts. In the region of Tafel linearity, the Tafel slope for methanation of CRD-Cu3Pd NCs is 74.9 mV decade−1, close to a value of 59 mV decade−1, manifesting a one-electron preequilibrium step prior to a ratelimiting non-electrochemical step. The Tafel slope for methanation on Cu foils is 118.8 mV decade−1, close to 118 mV decade−1, indicative of the single electron transfer step as the rate-limiting step in methanation (Figure 3a).[12a] The similar
trends were observed on C-Pd and FL-Pd3Cu NCs. The Tafel slope for CO conversion on FL-Pd3Cu is 60.2 mV decade−1, twothirds of 92.1 mV decade−1 of C-Pd (Figure 3b). The obviously decreased Tafel slope for FL-Pd3Cu is advantageous, for a lesser potential shift can cause a greater logarithmic increase in CO partial current density.[16]
To get a further understanding on the origin of enhanced catalytic activity, DFT calculations were conducted. The proposed reaction pathway is described in Figure 4a. CO2 first absorbs on the surface of catalysts and protonates to form *COOH intermediate. Then *COOH is reduced to absorbed *CO. On the FL-Pd3Cu catalysts, the final product CO is subsequently obtained. While on the CRD-Cu3Pd surfaces, the *CO converts to the intermediate *CHO, *CH2O, and *CH3O step by step, and finally form CH4. Figure 4b shows the free energy (ΔG) diagram for FL-Pd3Cu, pure flower-like Pd (FL-Pd), and C-Pd, respectively. Based on the previous study, binding energy of *COOH determines the overpotential because the uphill energy barrier of the first proton-coupled electron transfer step is needed to be overcome.[17] The ΔG to form *COOH for Pd3Cu (211), Pd (211), and Pd (111) have slight differences. Subsequently, the second proton-coupled electron transfer occurs more facilely because of the downhill energy barrier during this process. More importantly, the ΔG required for the ease of CO differs significantly in the increasing sequence from Pd3Cu (211) to Pd (111), followed by Pd (211). The easier desorption of CO from Pd3Cu (211) leads to excellent CO selectivity of FL-Pd3Cu. As the CO adsorption strengthening, the CO selectivity decreases for C-Pd and FL-Pd.

Figure 4c shows the ΔG for CRD-Cu3Pd NCs and Cu foil. Introduction of steps and kinks to the atomically flat surfaces has been proven to be favorable for promoting methane production in CO2ER.[18] However, there is no detailed explanation about methane production on high-index facets of Pd–Cu alloy. According to our DFT calculations, the adsorption of intermediate *CHO is much stronger than that of *COH, so we consider *CHO as the intermediate for CH4 formation. Apparently, Cu3Pd (211) exhibits a much lower energy barrier for COOH* formation than that of Cu (111), which contributes a lot to the lower onset potential for CH4 of CRD-Cu3Pd NCs. Moreover, the uphill energy barrier from *CO to *CHO for Cu3Pd (211) is 0.12 eV lower than that of Cu (111). Neglecting the second step of downhill energy barrier, Cu3Pd (211) takes apparent advantage on CH4 formation compared to Cu (111). The other reaction models are shown in Figure S9 (Supporting Information). In summary, we synthesized Pd–Cu bimetallic catalysts with high-index facets by a controllable one-pot route. The morphology of Pd–Cu NPs can be easily tuned with the adjustment of compositional ratio. Thanks to the alloy effect, a high CO current density covering a wide potential range was achieved on FL-Pd3Cu catalysts. In addition, the CRD-Cu3Pd catalysts exhibited a decreased onset potential and enhanced CH4 current density compared to Cu foil. The corresponding DFT calculation results demonstrated that the outstanding performance of CRD-Cu3Pd is attributed to both low coordinated sites and

sections.heading: Experimental Section
sections.text:
Materials: Cupric chloride dehydrate (CuCl2·2H2O, Tianjin Guangfu Technology Development Co. Ltd., 99.0%), sodium tetrachloropalladate (II) (Na2PdCl4, Energy Chemical, 99.95%), glucose (Tianjin Yuanli Technology Development Co. Ltd.), HDA (Tokyo Chemical Industry Co. Ltd., 90.0%), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, J&K Scientific Co. Ltd., 99.5%), and Cu foil (Sambo Corporation, 99.996%) were all used as received. Ultrapure (UP) water (18.2 MΩ cm) was used as the solvent throughout. Stock solutions of 100 × 10−3 m CuCl2·2H2O, 122.4 × 10−3 m Na2PdCl4, and 75.7 × 10−3 m glucose were prepared by dissolving 170 mg of CuCl2·2H2O, 360 mg of Na2PdCl4, and 150 mg of glucose into 10 mL of UP water, respectively.
Characterization: The morphology and structure of the products were characterized by TEM (JEM-2100). Concentration was detected by ICP-MS (7700x, Agilent). Electrochemical experiments were carried out using CHI 650D electrochemical analyzer (CHI Instrument, CHN)
Synthesis of Concave Rhombic Dodecahedral Cu3Pd: In a standard synthesis of CRD-Cu3Pd, 1.240 mL of aqueous CuCl2·2H2O (100 × 10−3 m), 0.335 mL of aqueous Na2PdCl4 (122.4 × 10−3 m), 200 mg of HDA, and 7 mL of UP water were added in a 20 mL glass vial. After the vial had been capped, the mixed solution was vigorously stirred at room temperature for 8 h. Subsequently, the solution was transferred to a 25 mL roundbottom flask. 1 mL of fresh aqueous glucose (75.7 × 10−3 m) was added before the flask was immersed into an oil bath and heated for 2 h under magnetic stirring. The final products were collected by centrifugation, washed four times with aqueous ethanol solution (20 vol%) and redispersed in 2 mL of UP water.
Synthesis of CuxPdy: Cu2Pd, CuPd, CuPd2, CuPd3 NPs were synthesized by almost the same procedure as Cu3Pd, except the usage of precursors. The details are listed in Table S1 (Supporting Information).
Preparation of Cu Foil: The Cu foil was first burnished by a piece of sandpaper to peel off the oxide layer on the surface and then ultrasonicated in ethanol and UP water for 15 min, respectively. After that, the Cu foil was immersed in H3PO4 solution with a piece of Pt foil as counter electrode. The electrochemical treatment was conducted under 1.5 V versus counter electrode for 30 min. After electrochemical polishing, the Cu foil was rinsed extensively with UP water and dried in ambient air.
Electrode Preparation: 5 wt% Vulcan XC-72R carbon black and 2 vol% Nafion solution were added into catalyst solutions and were ultrasonicated together for 30 min. Meanwhile, the glassy carbon electrode was carefully polished and washed with UP water before every experiment. Subsequently, certain volume of the aqueous suspension containing 0.05 mg catalysts was dropped onto the surface of the glassy carbon electrode with a geometric area of 0.5027 cm2 and later dried in an oven at 80 °C for 30 min.
Electrochemical Test: Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2ER) measurements were carried out in a gas-tight two-compartment electrochemical cell separated by a piece of Nafion-115 proton exchange membrane. Before the reaction, the cathode and anode compartment were filled with 100 mL of the electrolyte (0.1 m KHCO3). The electrode chambers were connected to a gas circulation system with a ten-port value (VICI) for on-line sampling to a gas chromatograph (Ruimin GC 2060, Shanghai). The gas circulation system was primarily made of stainless steel tubing and a homemade gas pump for the circulation of the gas. A mechanical pump was connected into the system to exhaust the carrier gas of the gas chromatograph when switch back the ten-port value. A pressure gauge was also connected into the system to monitor the gas pressure. The total volume of the gas in the circulation system after filling the reactor with electrolyte was 140 mL. Before the start of the reaction, both the electrolyte and circulation system were purged with
CO2 (≥99.995%) for 40 min to achieve CO2 saturation and remove air. Then the system was sealed and the initial CO2 pressure was kept atmospheric. There was no more CO2 purged into the closed system during the reaction. The gases in the closed circulation system were continuously circulated through the electrolyte for the entire reaction period.
A saturated Ag/AgCl and a platinum foil (2 × 2 cm2) were used as the reference electrode and the counter electrode, respectively. All potentials were measured against an Ag/AgCl reference electrode and converted to the RHE reference scale using E (vs RHE) = E (vs Ag/AgCl) + 0.21 V + 0.0591 × pH.
Computational Details: Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) was used to perform calculations with the BEEF-vdW exchange– correlation functional.[19] Valence electrons were described by using a plane-wave basis set with the cut-off energy of 400 eV. Meanwhile, core electrons were treated using projector augmented-wave method.[20] The Monkhorst–Pack k-points grid (5 × 5 × 1) was used to sample the Brillouin zone of the surface.[21] The electronic occupancies were determined according to the Methfessel–Paxton scheme with an energy smearing of 0.15 eV and the total energies were evaluated by extrapolating to zero broadening. The dipole correction was included in the direction perpendicular to the slab surface. A global optimization was performed to identify the preferred alloy structure. Then, the slabs (Pd (111): 2 × 2 × 5, Cu (111):3 × 3 × 4 and (211) surfaces: (3 × 2 × 5)) were built with top two layers relaxed. All structures were optimized until the force on each atom has been less than 0.02 eV Å−1.
